questions.question: How do DRY and SOLID basics apply in Ruby?
questions.title: DRY and SOLID Basics in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) and SOLID are design principles for changeable code. In Ruby: DRY means extract a repeated method or validation to one place; SOLID shows up as small classes with one responsibility (SRP), modules for sharing behavior (over deep inheritance), and dependency injection (pass the logger in, don't hardcode it). The Ruby twist: duck typing and modules let you satisfy LSP/ISP/DIP lightly — you don't need formal interfaces; if two objects respond to the same methods, they're interchangeable. Apply the principles pragmatically: extract real duplication, keep classes focused, prefer modules over inheritance, and inject dependencies — but don't over-engineer simple code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can map DRY/SOLID onto Ruby idioms (modules over inheritance, duck typing for LSP/ISP, DI by passing objects), pragmatically.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forcing Java-style interfaces in Ruby (use modules/duck typing), or over-engineering simple code with patterns.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: DRY = one source of truth; SOLID in Ruby = small classes (SRP), modules over inheritance, duck typing for LSP/ISP, DI by injection. Pragmatic, not rigid.

sections.title: Principles in Ruby Idioms
sections.content: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) and SOLID are design principles for changeable code. In Ruby, DRY means extract a repeated method or validation to one place; SOLID shows up as small classes with one responsibility (SRP), modules for sharing behavior over deep inheritance, and dependency injection — pass the logger in, don't hardcode it. The Ruby twist: duck typing and modules let you satisfy LSP, ISP, and DIP lightly — you don't need formal interfaces; if two objects respond to the same methods, they're interchangeable, which is duck typing covering LSP and ISP. Apply the principles pragmatically: extract real duplication, keep classes focused, prefer modules over inheritance, and inject dependencies — but don't over-engineer simple code.

sections.title: Principles -> Ruby Idioms
sections.content:
DRY -> extract; SRP -> small classes; LSP/ISP -> duck typing/modules; DIP -> inject.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D[DRY: extract] --> S[SRP: small classes]
  S --> M[modules over inheritance]
  M --> Di[DIP: inject the dependency]
```

sections.title: DRY and SOLID in Ruby
sections.content:
```ruby
# DRY: extract a repeated validation to one place
class User
  validate_email :email   # one shared method, used by many models
end

# SRP: a class does one thing (split formatting out of the exporter)
class InvoiceExporter; def export(i); to_pdf(i); end; end
class InvoiceFormatter; def format(i); # ... ; end; end

# Modules over deep inheritance (share behavior without a deep tree)
module Trackable; def track(event); # ...; end; end
class Order; include Trackable; end
class Shipment; include Trackable; end   # both get .track

# DIP: inject the logger (don't hardcode it)
class OrderProcessor
  def initialize(logger: Logger.new); @logger = logger; end
end
# OrderProcessor.new(logger: Rails.logger)  # inject a different one

# Duck typing (LSP/ISP): if it quacks, it's fine
def send_notice(obj); obj.notify; end   # works for any object with notify
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forcing Java-style formal interfaces in Ruby (use modules and duck typing).
Over-engineering simple code with patterns — apply principles pragmatically.
Deep inheritance trees where a module would share the behavior cleanly.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: DRY = one source of truth; in Ruby, extract a repeated method/validation.
SRP = small classes with one responsibility (split concerns into classes).
Prefer modules over deep inheritance to share behavior (include Trackable).
Duck typing covers LSP/ISP: if objects respond to the same methods, they swap.
DIP = inject dependencies (logger:) instead of hardcoding them; pragmatic, not rigid.

sections.content: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) and SOLID are design principles for changeable code. In Ruby, DRY means extract a repeated method or validation to one place; SOLID shows up as small classes with one responsibility, SRP, modules for sharing behavior over deep inheritance, and dependency injection — pass the logger in, don't hardcode it. The Ruby twist: duck typing and modules let you satisfy LSP, ISP, and DIP lightly — you don't need formal interfaces; if two objects respond to the same methods, they're interchangeable, which is duck typing covering LSP and ISP. Apply the principles pragmatically: extract real duplication, keep classes focused, prefer modules over inheritance, and inject dependencies — but don't over-engineer simple code. A common mistake is forcing Java-style formal interfaces in Ruby, and over-engineering simple code with patterns.
